newsitem.title: INDIA: India party heads for split in rebel convention.
newsitem.headline: India party heads for split in rebel convention.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's party appeared set for a split on Saturday as rebels led by its president, Laloo Prasad Yadav, prepared to hold a convention.

Witnesses said supporters of Yadav began assembling at the building housing the New Delhi office of the populous eastern state of Bihar, of which Yadav is the chief minister. Speeches were scheduled to start at 12.30 p.m.(0700 GMT), an aide of Yadav said.
At the meeting, Yadav was expected to launch a breakaway group of the centre-left Janata Dal that heads India's ruling 15-party alliance, the United Front.

The odd instance of the president turning rebel rattled the ruling party, but there was no threat for Gujral's two-month-old government from Yadav, who has announced that his group would under no circumstance withdraw support to Gujral.

Supporters of Yadav, a powerful low-caste leader and chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar, boycotted elections for the party's presidency held on Thursday, alleging that voters' list had been rigged.
Yadav was pitted against Sharad Yadav, no relative of his but a fellow low-caste socialist leader, in the first leadership election in the nine-year-old party.
Results of the ballotting are expected on Sunday.
Laloo Yadav's differences are mainly with former prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda, who Yadav's supporters say played an unfair role in an effort to dislodge their leader.
Gujral, who has not publicly taken sides in the leadership battle, is believed to be neutral in the power struggle.
"There is no danger to the government. If the prime minister is ever in trouble, then Laloo Yadav will be the first to jump up and help him," the party president said on Friday.
Laloo Yadav held a meeting with Gujral late on Friday night, but there was no indication of any breakthrough in a last minute effort by senior leaders to avert a split in the ranks.
Janata Dal has 45 lawmakers in the 545-seat lower house, Lok Sabha, in which the United Front has an overall 178 members, most of whom from regional groups or leftist allies.
Yadav's support base is believed to be at least 16 members, and his supporters put the figure at 24.

The ruling coalition's life-breath is the Congress party, India's oldest political machine, whose 140 deputies offer make-or-break support to the government in an axis formed to keep out the Hindu nationalists, who control 194 votes.
Gujral became prime minister in April after the Congress forced Deve Gowda's government to fall and renewed support to the coalition on the condition that it changed its leader.

Laloo Yadav is also embroiled in a $280-million "fodder" scandal, in which the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has indicted him among 56 politicians and officials named in alleged embezzlement of state animal welfare funds.
Yadav says he is innocent, and alleges that the CBI is helping his political rivals. He has refused to resign as Bihar's chief minister and face trial on corruption charges.
Senior Janata Dal leaders have been worried by the loss of image which is believed to have resulted from the scandal.
